paragraphs.text: Again, an exhortation to the solitary brothers by Mar Abraham of Nathpar: The reason for the solitary way of life, written by him for someone who asked him [?].
Because I saw that you were eager to walk on the road that leads

to eternal life, which our Savior Christ opened up, O my true friends, I wanted first to say a little about it before you, and then fulfill your request in practice, if God grants [?]. Since, then, the good planting of the love of virtue had been planted in you, you not only listened gladly to my words but also urged me to set down in writing what I had said before you [?]. Having agreed to this request of yours, I thought it good to arrange this account for you in chapters, first explaining its reason: why, when God saw fit that we should first be in this way of life and afterward receive another from him, he allowed us to grow up in this way of life and in their conduct in that way of life [?]. From the outset I wanted this to be the beginning. Chapter One: [?] It is not for everyone to enter this way of life. Chapter Two: Concerning those who draw near [?]— with what thoughts and deeds they ought to approach. Chapter Three: Once they have entered, how they ought to walk in it. Chapter Four: When trials and struggles confront them, what they should do. Chapter Five: If they happen to fall, how they should rise again. Chapter Six: What vigilance and diligence are required of those who walk on this road. Introduction: [?] the reason for this way of life. I will now begin with the help of your prayers, first explaining the reason for this way of life, as I promised, and beginning a little further back. If we had been made immortal and not subject to change by God from the beginning, we would have possessed good things like animals, that is, without reason, and we would not have been able to enjoy them, because we would not previously have experienced and learned through comparison with evil [?]. Nor could we have implanted knowledge of them in ourselves naturally, because they are not among the things naturally implanted [?]. Evidence of this can be seen in the bee, [?], and ants, together with the rest of the [?] creatures. They each possess something [?], and because it is natural, they are not aware of it. Nor could this have been so [?]:

that, if he had given us knowledge of these things by nature, we could have enjoyed them with discernment. Unless, perhaps, we were to claim the divine rank for ourselves in our presumption! For he alone knows everything without comparison and without instruction, because his nature, too, is without beginning and beyond comparison. He precedes everything [?], and he always knows everything without experience and without instruction. Again, if he had given us knowledge of these things by nature, we would have known nothing else except what was sufficient for us [?]. For we would not have understood his ordering of things, nor his varied wisdom, which [?] in many ways and through necessities. We would have been deprived of much knowledge. But now, in his indescribable wisdom, he first made us mortal and subject to change, and our knowledge grows through these [?]. For this reason he arranged this world in such a way that it would teach us about its Maker. For through the contrasts and variations of the natures within it, and their changes in relation to one another [?]. He did not make our nature simple—that is, either soul alone or body— but composed it of two unequal parts [?], body and soul. And to each of the parts [?] of our nature he gave something suited to it [?]. To the soul, along with knowledge and reason, he gave love for good things. To the body, however, he gave a strong inclination toward visible things [?], so that from this an unceasing battle and struggle might arise. A person would thus have to struggle with himself in practicing goodness, as the blessed Paul says: “For I delight in the law of God in the inner person.” “But I see another law in my members, waging war against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin that is in my members.” Through that unceasing battle, the soul would acquire [?] a greater love for good things, so that the soul’s love for good things would not be without benefit.

Since we cannot bring it to complete fulfillment here because of the inclinations of mortality, he has prepared another world for us, filled with every abundant blessing. When we are there, we will practice goodness without struggle. This has been shown to us in our Savior Christ. For he did not merely teach us through his words, but also showed us in his own person through his deeds, and all believers [?] in an example. Those, then, who have learned about the mysteries of the world to come and the good things in it ought [?] to seek good things from now on. They do not choose those things out of contempt for these, as though these were contemptible. Rather, because their love for the things to come grows stronger, they leave behind these visible things, so that they may [?] still more in their love for the things to come. For freedom from the distractions arising from visible things draws them toward love and affection for God. For their meditation is not on visible things, but on those that are to come and are not visible. Constant reflection on those things kindles the mind still more. Let these remarks suffice concerning the reason for this way of life. Now I begin the discourses that we set out above. First discourse: Why it is not for everyone to undertake this way of life. Because many hardships and battles [?] confront anyone who wishes to walk on this path, I say that it is not for everyone to walk on it. For not everyone can endure the afflictions and hardships that confront a person on it. Anyone who wishes to walk on it encounters these. And this is enough to demonstrate what I have said: all its practices are contrary to nature. The hardships of anyone who lives contrary to nature are well known. Yet this path alone does not lead to the kingdom of heaven, nor does God require this way of life [?] from all human beings. Rather [?], there are many paths and various roads. For everyone is permitted [?] to choose one path according to their strength and walk on it. Our life-giver Christ bears witness to this when he says in the [?] parable of the seed: “That which fell on good ground and yielded [?]

fruit—some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, and some thirtyfold.” And again: “There are many rooms in my Father’s house.” Through these sayings he shows that the way of life of all human beings is not the same, nor are their rewards. But because this way of life is above nature, it is like someone who stands continually before the king: He needs vigilance. [?] the words of the king’s servants. Likewise, anyone who follows this way of life [?]. For he must not only keep himself free from sins in deeds, actions, and words, but must also continually maintain watchful thoughts. He must have a well-ordered mind. And it is clear how much difficulty there is in this way. For unless a person is continually watchful and on guard, he cannot become pure. And because not everyone is capable of it, I advise that not everyone should undertake it. Especially because of those [?] who do not even consider why they left the world and undertook this way of life, but approach it casually, as though it were something ordinary. Though they imagine that they are persevering, they are not persevering. And if even a little affliction happens to reach them, they abandon it and flee. They betray their first faith, as Paul the herald says. I have said these things not to prevent anyone who wishes to undertake it, but to advise him not to approach it casually, as though approaching something ordinary, but with knowledge and discernment. Chapter Two: With what thoughts and [?] those who undertake it ought to approach it. My lord, I advise anyone who wishes to travel along this way, because [?] mountains, cliffs, and robbers who plunder. To put it briefly, it is a narrow, constricted way, full of hardship, [?], and afflictions. It also resembles a reservoir full of water: if [?] breaches and holes appear in it, they drain the water from the reservoir and leave it empty. For this reason I advise that anyone who wishes to travel along it should enter it with knowledge and careful examination. And above all, he should choose the study of the divine Scriptures, for [?] has trodden the way and [?], and it can

show him signs and tokens that give confidence. From the Scriptures he can gather provisions that will bring him to the end of his journey. He should put foolish thoughts and a distracted mind far from himself, and refuse to listen to useless words employed by those whose knowledge is foolish, who say, ‘The study of the Scriptures produces conceit and arrogance.’ Let the person who says this understand: if a purgative medicine has such an effect, what will a measure of dates do? I have said these things not to declare that the study of the Scriptures does not become an occasion for arrogance in many people, but because these people resemble someone [?] for whom the purgative he is given [?]. For his constitution is marked by sickness, and its foundations are not sound. His whole nature has become twisted and crooked. And when the intention of his purpose is not upright and pure, his actions are not pure either. But let us reject this thought and drive it away from ourselves. Let us understand that, just as no one can cross the vast sea without a boat or a ship, nor can anyone enter a fierce battle and come out unharmed when he is unarmed, or does not even know how to throw [?], so no one can enter this merciless battle and come out unharmed. From the Scriptures he learns what sins are and what righteousness is. The evil one fights against him, and from them he learns the evil one’s wicked devices, which are continually being arranged against us. From them he is trained to shoot arrows against him. From them he can learn what his way is and where it leads, whether to the right or to the left. From them [?] those things that deceive him. From them he is trained, if possible, to be shrewd as a serpent and innocent as a dove. And greatest of all, from them he learns the true faith, rightly confessed in the Trinity of worshipful persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one power that holds all things and governs all things.

[?] I said, O [?], not because I despair of the help of divine grace. But understand what I am saying. If someone has excelled in good deeds toward God without studying Scripture, understand this too: if someone has excelled without study, how much more would he have excelled through study! But although grace helps in every way, I follow the order of [?]. Let him continually reflect on the world and its changing circumstances [?], considering the hardships and exhausting labors it imposes on its inhabitants. Let him rise in thought to kings and descend to beggars, and see that they have all fallen into the same exhausting toil. Kings toil for their dominions, rulers for themselves, the rich for their wealth, and the poor because of their poverty. Who can recount its troubles and afflictions, and [?] its childish inclination toward every evil? A person grows rich and becomes proud. He becomes poor and envious. He hungers and thirsts. He eats his fill and becomes wanton. He gains authority and becomes puffed up. He is humbled and blasphemes. Its joys do not last. Its punishments are endless. Its pleasure lasts only the blink of an eye. Its sighs are unending, and its exhausting labors are beyond counting. Its [?], and there is no help. Its inhabitants are worn out in body and worn out in soul: the rich by their worries and the poor by their labor. Thieves wait for a chance to steal, and guards keep watch through their sleepless nights. The rich look for bribes, and the poor devise ways to offer bribes. A person runs about and acquires treasures [?], so that he may enjoy them and rest. But instead they make him a weary slave of distress. He longs for sleep but is afraid. He craves silver and [?]. For its sake he [?] on the roads. For its sake he goes down to the sea. For its sake he is killed by thieves. For its sake he climbs mountains. For its sake [?] the joy of wealth, even for a full hour—I do not know it. But greatest of all, what seems greater than all the rest is itself still more distressing. Keep recalling these things continually, my lord, so that you may [?] love of the world from your mind. I have said these things for the weak. Turn, my lord, and look at the children of

angels: see, they are scraping up refuse! And look at the children of the kingdom: see, they are distracted in the marketplace! Turn your gaze toward [?] Christ’s inheritance: see, they are quarreling over a boundary! Look at those for whom heavenly rewards are kept: see, they are wandering after moneybags! O people, why is your discernment blind? His father wore himself out and left it behind, and now his son has taken up his exhausting toil. His father went away and drowned, and now his son is running after him. What did your father gain from his exhausting toil, you fool, that you are now running along his road? Turn, my lord, and look at those who love God. Those others are distressed while they are rich; these rejoice while they give their possessions away. Those others grieve while they receive crowns; these rejoice while they are battered. And when they are persecuted, they rejoice. Those others mourn while they reign; these exult while they are being killed. Prepare yourself for every trial, so that when trials encounter you, you do not give up and flee. Keep away from all bodily possessions, so that concerns about them do not hinder you from traveling on your way. Despise bodily concerns, so that they do not confuse your paths and [?]. Draw near, armed with all these things. And draw near with trust in your Creator, casting all your care upon him—not by becoming slack, but by firmly establishing your resolve, courageously, like a warrior, with both your hands resting on the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left—that is, amid things that distress you and things that gladden you, amid praise and [?]. Do not let your thoughts be divided: “Can I do it? If not, I will turn back.” Do not let the evil one unsettle you and lead you away like a captive. Continually reflect on what is written: “Do not approach her with a divided heart.” And again, on that other saying: “If you approach the fear of God, surrender yourself to every trial.” Let your foundation be laid as upon a rock, upon the humility of [?]. And how those who draw near ought to conduct themselves. If, then, you have drawn near, my lord, armed, with your foundation laid upon the rock of truth, and have strengthened your mind like a warrior,

like a mighty fighter, like a sower and like a reaper, having taken up your Lord’s yoke and carrying your cross upon your shoulder, and have cast away from yourself the world and its desires, and have loved our Lord and his glory, and become poor in all visible things, then you will become an heir of the good things to come. And while you are mortal in your body, you will mingle in your thoughts with the companies of the angels; and while you are on earth, you will be like someone in heaven [?]. Therefore, in your conduct, make yourself dead to all visible things, and set purity of soul before your eyes as your goal. For this all who fear God have longed, and after it they have run. Let your conduct be directed toward it by every means. Do not begin with great things, lest you end with small things. Instead, begin with small things, so that you may attain great things. Let your fasting be moderate, with [?] discernment, knowing that it is not abstinence from food in and of itself that God seeks, but fasting undertaken for a fitting purpose—that is, to subdue the passions of desire. For a person cannot otherwise put his thoughts in order unless he restrains his desires. For just as an unruly horse cannot be subdued without a bridle and bit, so the body cannot be subjected to the soul unless its desires have first been subdued. Along with the fasting of the body, acquire the fasting of the soul as well. That is, fast from pride and hatred, which are the mothers of many sins. For from them are born murderous envy and destructive [?], and the rest of the other sins. Let it be a symbol of the fasting after the resurrection, when we will be entirely without sins. Let your service, too, be moderate and discerning. Know that God is pleased not by a great number of psalms, but by an alert mind that gazes at him in wonder. Do not expect to acquire this state of mind immediately, at once. Only a few have attained it, and [?] great labors. But I have said these things so that your mind will not be occupied only with the service of psalms, but will also be mingled with meditation

on God, even if not entirely. For just as someone cannot travel swiftly along a road without setting a goal for where he is going, so someone cannot attain this wonder in God, which comes, as it were, in spiritual stages, without first setting it before himself as a goal. If distraction comes upon you while you are standing at the service, and you try to gather your thoughts but they will not gather, sit down and stir yourself to weeping or plaintive cries, saying against your enemy, “Even if in one way you have disturbed me [?], in another I give thanks to God.” Do not be distressed in your mind and say that you have not performed the service. For, as I said, God is not pleased merely by the recitation of psalms. You also know that the psalms are recited for this reason: so that, through the recitation of the great words in [?], our mind may be awakened and turn its gaze toward God. By every [?], my lord, take care not to give distress a place in your mind for a long time, lest it lead you to despondency. And distraction of mind will rob you of your labors. When you are distressed [?], let your distress be moderate. If you are sitting in solitude and many varied thoughts arise within you, do not say, “I am wasting my time,” and consequently let sorrow rule over you and leave your cell. Instead, wait in hope and remember that joy comes after distress, and rest after hardship. Love solitude, then, above everything, for it will bring you to purity of soul, if you desire it. For just as it is impossible to cross the great sea, as I said, without a boat or a ship, so it is impossible for someone to attain purity of soul easily without solitude. And just as someone cannot see his face in water unless it is clear, so someone cannot see his faults and cleanse them without solitude. And just as someone cannot enter a city fortified with great, strong walls except by entering through its gates, so someone cannot attain

purity of soul unless he drives all his faults away from himself. The very expression “purity of soul” signifies this: cleansing from every fault. And just as it is impossible [?] for someone to see his face in a dirty mirror unless it is polished, so someone cannot attain the vision and wonder of God unless he first cleanses all his faults from his soul. These things I was [?]. See, my son, do not confine your way of life to abstaining from food and reciting psalms. when the divine vision and the constant [?] of his greatness are not mingled with them. For just as someone who tends the winds gains nothing, according to the saying of the fathers, so it is with someone whose way of life is confined to these things. I say these things not to suggest that those things should be absent, but that these things too should accompany them. For those things are outward, involving only the body, whereas these things take place inwardly, in the mind and in the soul’s love. Therefore, be armed with these inward [?]: the subduing of evil passions and the dawning of the love of God. Again I advise you: be [?] at the door of the cell of a man pure in soul, so that there you may lay down [?]. Chapter [?]. And if a battle should arise against [?]—[?], O man—a battle should arise against you, do not become confused and disturbed. Instead, shelter your mind in endurance. Without it, not one of those who fear God has been found pleasing to him. Bring to your mind the afflictions of the prophets, the sufferings of the martyrs, and the persecution of the righteous. Some of them were stoned, and some were sawn apart. Some were killed, some were cut to pieces, some were burned, and some were [?]. To put it briefly, not one of them received his crown without endurance. Remember Paul too, who cries out that, along with all these things, there must be endurance, without which no one sees [?]. Remember those who love God: not one of them completed his course in ease, but amid various afflictions. Along with these, bring to mind the people of this world: not one of them achieves the fulfillment of his desire without toil. Some of them fall into the seas;

[?] some climb mountains for gold; some travel difficult roads for fleeting wealth and empty praise. And if this is how things are with them, how much more must those who pursue heavenly wealth and imperishable treasures and delight that never ends endure afflictions and toils for its sake [?] until they attain it, wearing the breastplate of faith, with which they can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. And remember that enduring command of Jesus Christ: “By your endurance you will gain your souls.” And again he said, “Whoever endures to the end will be saved.” Bringing these things to mind, O [?], stand courageously and do not be afraid. Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will deliver you. Give yourself continually to prayer, without losing heart. And if you are not readily heard, [?] God allows this for your benefit, so that your endurance may become known, not to him, but to us, and also to put the demons to shame. And if a battle of thoughts should arise against you, know that, if you do not desire it, it is like a passerby. And if a battle of passions should arise against you, go to brothers you know and receive encouragement. Do not be disturbed by the demons when they show you apparitions, but rouse yourself. to prayer, and ask God; immediately they leave and flee. But do not leave your cell during your trials. For just as a person may squander the work of an entire year because of a little hardship that comes upon him, so it is with someone who has maintained solitude for some time, but in this small struggle, after which a great and strong [?] of peace is to come, he leaves and flees. And in our trials, always remember [?]. Also keep the good things constantly in mind, and reflect on the torments. For thinking about these things will relieve you of much hardship. And remember this briefly: today hardship, tomorrow rest. And readily

you are strengthened by the hidden power of God [?]. For if [?] and they fall, how will they rise? If it happens that you fall, my brother, do not remain in despair [?] and return to the world. Instead, remember that your Lord is merciful and welcomes those who have gone astray when they repent. Do not forget what was said by Christ, who gives us life: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” Remember the parable about the prodigal son, in which he reveals God's mercy: how he welcomes sinners when they repent and gives them a share in good things. And again, the parable about the widow who had lost her coin: how she rejoiced over it. And again, the sheep that was lost; and again, the saying, “The healthy do not need a physician, but those who are seriously ill.” And again, remember Paul, who cries out: “The saying is trustworthy: Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost, so that in me first Jesus Christ might display all his patience.” And again, what was said by our Lord himself: “If your brother sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day returns to you and says, ‘I have sinned,’ accept him.” And bring forward testimonies resembling these, including accounts of deeds. Begin with the blessed David, and come down to the heralds of the New Covenant. You will find among them those who denied him, like Simon, and tax collectors, like Matthew, and persecutors, like Paul. Through these people God showed that he has opened the door of repentance to sinners. I remember that prostitute whose sins were forgiven through her tears, and that leader of the Corinthians who fell into a great and grievous sin. Through a little repentance he was forgiven; moreover, they restored his former rank to him. But why do I restrict my words to small examples? Look at the whole church, which was gathered from none other than pagans who provoked God and Jews who crucified him. As you remember these things, my lord, stand firm in trust in your Maker's mercy. Do not waver in your mind and say, “I will not be forgiven; and even if I am forgiven, my former rank

I will not attain.” Do not let that doubt cast you into the pit of [?], that is, into sins worse than the former ones. Instead, call the blessed David to mind. After he received forgiveness for his sin [?] through the prophet, what does he cry out and say? “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath.” While he was [?] because of the sin I committed, O my Lord, worthy [?], I am worthy to be disciplined. But I ask that you not forget me forever.” And again, in another psalm: “My wounds have become foul and festered because of my foolishness. I was greatly shaken.” By these words he shows [?] his persecutors [?] his sin [?] was forgiven. And again: “Lord, all my longing is before you, and my sighs are not hidden from you.” As though he were saying [?], “Lord, forgive me my sins.” Remember these things at all times, my lord, if you happen to be overcome by the weakness of human nature and fall. And when you get up, rely firmly on our Lord’s mercies with all your heart, and he will help you. [?] How vigilance and diligence are required in this way of life. Concerning vigilance and diligence, my lord, I think that many words are unnecessary, because the benefit they bring is well known. But so that it may be known how useful they are for this way of life, I will say a few words about them, speaking first about the harm caused by negligence and laziness, so that, by comparison with them, it may be known how necessary vigilance and diligence are. I begin my discourse with the words of [?], who spoke as follows: “My son, if you sleep a little, slumber a little, and place your hand on your chest a little, then poverty will come upon you, and need will overtake you like a diligent man.” First [?]

let us take care to explain these words [?] so that they may be understood by us. Since human nature loves rest, my lord, whenever the will gives nature a little room, nature then carries out its own work. It is like giving a hand to a lame person: then he walks. So too, if the will becomes a little negligent and gives nature room, nature then carries out its own work. This is what the wise man said: if you become a little negligent and give room to drowsiness—that is, to nature—nature then carries out its own work, namely, that you fall asleep. And when nature has had its fill of this one kind, it then throws you into another. This is what is meant by, “Place your hand on your chest a little.” What, then, happens to this person? “Then poverty will come upon you, and need will overtake you.” These mean the same thing. By repeating the expression, he showed how ugly and contemptible it is. That is, you become destitute [?] of all good things. And if you possess anything, you lose it. He aptly said, “a diligent man”—that is, diligent in idleness and negligence. And after all this he concluded his discourse with the foolish man: “You are a fool [?], because, although you could have been diligent and active in good things, [?].” Have you seen what this wise man said about negligence, diligence, and laziness? Listen to what he says again in another place: “I passed by the field of a lazy man, and by the vineyard of a man lacking understanding.” It all grew over [?] and became filled with bitter weeds and thorns, and weeds covered its surface. So too is a person: an empty vineyard of righteousness. Through his negligence and lack of diligence, a thicket grows in him, with many [?] that come upon him without his knowing. [?] Like moles they make their home in him. Or who does not know how many [?] were snatched from the hands of kings, their masters, by their enemies? How many people's houses have burned down! How many ships have sunk! Through lack of vigilance, weariness, and lack of diligence. Keep remembering these things and things like them, my lord. Do not rely on your labors of long ago, and say, 'I no longer need

vigilance.' Who can remember the blessed David, a blameless and righteous man, and the slight negligence he showed concerning [?] his eyes— how he stumbled and fell into a great sin—and not be afraid and tremble and remain vigilant at all times? If you wish to escape, my lord, listen to my words, and you will be able to save your soul. Constantly station guards at the gate of your thoughts, so that you do not think things that are not in accordance with God's will. Station guards over your mouth, so that it does not speak an evil word against your brothers. Keep guards stationed over your eyes, so that they do not look about wantonly, and over your hearing, so that your ears do not hear foolish sounds and your thoughts become troubled. Weigh your words in a balance, my lord, so that you speak what is necessary and when it is necessary. If you observe these things, my lord, you will be able to save yourself and those who know you. Let this little illustration remain in our memory, my lord. Just as a farmer should not trust that his crop will escape unharmed until [?] into the storehouses, so a person should not place confidence in his deeds until the time of his death. Truth is a light in which there is no darkness. Before all your deeds, acquire truth, and before all your labors, acquire faith. For everyone who does all his deeds in truth brings his deeds to a good end. And everyone who performs his labors in faith— faith lends him a hand in every holy labor. If someone tells you, “I have the truth,” but has no truthful deeds, he is a liar, and there is no truth in him. And if anyone tells you that someone who eats and drinks his fill, wears fine clothes, and puts on luxurious shoes, and lives with women who serve him, maintains chastity, he is a liar; do not believe him. For everyone

who devotes himself to eating meat and drinking wine is a worker of sexual immorality. Scripture also bears witness to this when it says: “Everyone who sows in his flesh reaps corruption from his flesh.” For nothing is sown without sprouting, nor is anything conceived without being born, nor is anything planted without coming up. Nothing is concealed without being revealed, and nothing is hidden without becoming known. For all a person's secrets come to light, and all people's hidden things come into the open. All their secrets are disclosed before every generation. The wicked are ashamed of their wicked deeds, and the righteous rejoice in their righteous deeds. For just as these visible bodily deeds of wickedness corrupt this visible body, so too these hidden evils, which cannot be seen, corrupt the soul, which cannot be seen. And if someone tells you that anyone who lives with his father and mother and acquires gold and silver amid worldly cares and worldly concerns, and amid the deception of fleeting wealth, is a disciple of Christ, he is a liar; do not believe him. But if you believe him, you make these words of Christ false, for he said: “Anyone who does not give up everything he has cannot be my disciple.” And: “Anyone who does not leave his father and mother, his brothers and sisters, and take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” For no one can become a disciple of Christ unless he has placed himself in his [?], learned his craft, taken up his cross, shared in his sufferings, and entered into the pattern of his death. Therefore, everyone who possesses this world is a disciple of the world, and everyone who has freed himself from this world is a disciple of Christ. For this reason, if you bear the name of Christian, conduct yourself in a manner befitting [?]. Labor for the sake of your name, so that you do not dishonor Christianity by your deeds. And if you bear the name of virginity and chastity, do deeds that accord with your name, and do not dishonor the name of virginity by your evil conduct. And if you are a member of the covenant, keep your covenant with a good reputation. The covenant that you keep will itself keep you. If you are not watchful over yourself, you will fall away from

your covenant, and fiery Gehenna will receive you. For this reason, if you wish to maintain true chastity, put on the armor of fasting and show courage in ascetic discipline. Strengthen yourself through endurance. Afflict yourself with hunger, constrain your body with thirst, and dry up the veins of your blood. For holiness shines in a lean and wasted body, and purity rejoices in emaciated flesh. But in moist and well-fed bodies, the fire of sexual immorality burns. Therefore, if you are fighting for the crown of holiness, you must enter the contest and struggle against your body's desire and against the [?] of your thoughts. You must win the inward contest and the outward battle, and fight against the sights of the daytime and against sleep at night. For there is no crown without a contest, no victory without battle, and no harvest without irrigation, no wages without work, no rest without toil, no comfort without mourning, and no relief without distress. For everyone who leaves this world for Christ's sake will go and inherit the world to come, which he promised to the holy ones. Everyone who leaves an earthly kingdom will go and inherit the kingdom of heaven. Everyone who leaves his bodily father will go and become a son of the Father in heaven. Everyone who leaves his mother in the flesh will go and become a son of the Holy Spirit. Everyone who leaves brothers and sisters will go and become a brother of Christ. Everyone who leaves an earthly table will go and enjoy the table of the kingdom. Everyone who leaves an earthly bridal chamber will enter the bridal chamber of light. Everyone who leaves earthly wealth acquires heavenly wealth. Everyone who leaves his city and his village will go and inherit Jerusalem in heaven. Therefore, everyone who leaves possessions that perish, a building that falls, clothes that wear out, beauty that fades, splendor that passes away, and adornment that comes to nothing, youth that turns into old age, and joy that changes into sorrow, will go and receive in exchange for them, in the world that does not pass away, rest that never ends, fullness that never [?], beauty that never fades, youth that never grows old, and childhood that never changes, a garment of glory and a crown of light, a robe of honor and a royal diadem that never passes away or [?], forever. But if you wish to win the contest of holiness and be crowned with the crown of virginity, let your entire battle be against your own soul,

and your entire struggle against your body's desire. Restrain your soul from what it asks for, and deprive it of what it craves. Do not follow its advice, and do not listen to its disturbances. Do not follow its enticements or believe its promises. Do not let it mislead you with its many words. For it speaks but does not act; it promises but does not fulfill. It swears but does not keep its word; it makes agreements and deals treacherously with them. It keeps you hanging on empty hope and makes you rely on worthless confidence. It fears fasting and slips away from keeping vigil. It despises frequent prayers. It is deceitful and takes refuge in bodily pains and illnesses. It flees from spiritual work and takes refuge in bodily activities. It fears confinement and flees from recollection of the mind. It loves amusement and play, and the distraction of evil thoughts. It clings to [?] and flies through the air. It abandons the divine goad that lifts it to the lofty heights of heaven, and follows evil spirits, which plunge it into the depths below. It flees from those who take hold of it to lift it up. And she follows those who drag her down into the depths below. She fears instruction and runs away from discipline. She hates those who rebuke her and loves those who praise her. She runs away from the chaste and attaches herself to the dissolute. She hates silence and loves the diversion of idle talk. She runs away from hearing the words of God. And she longs to hear worldly stories. When she hears the words of the Holy Scriptures, she grows weary and falls asleep. But when she hears entertaining talk, she is alert and rejoices. When she stands at the vigil, her strength fails [?], and she loses her alertness [?]. But when she goes to work, her mind awakens and grows strong. At the prospect of fasting, she puts on a gloomy face. She hates spiritual pleasure and loves bodily pleasure. She fears the spiritual labor that enriches her. And she loves the labor of bodily comforts that impoverish her. She is awake to bodily things that kill her, and asleep to spiritual things that give her life. When you give her rest, she is not satisfied. And when you promise her pleasures, she does not say, “Enough.” When you deprive her of many pleasures, she asks you for small ones [?]. And when you give her small ones, she asks you for great ones. When she gains relief from afflictions, she asks you for a few pleasures. The more you let her loose, the farther down she descends. And when you pull

on her, she rises upward. Above, the bond of the rational mind [?] draws her to ascend. And below, the body's desire hangs upon her to make her descend. For bodily things are very easy for her, while spiritual things are very difficult for her. Such is the nature of the soul with which we are clothed. Therefore, do not listen to her. And even if she is not familiar with you, do not trust her, lest she lead you astray. For her speeches and explanations are many. Concerning bodily things, she urges you to have them happen quickly; but concerning spiritual things, she keeps you waiting with empty hope. As for food, drink, sleep, and rest, she urges you to put them into practice quickly. But as for keeping vigil, fasting, and prayer, she promises them for a distant time and does not carry them out. And everything she promises is false [?]. And everyone who trusts her in everything she tells him, she [?], and leaves him empty and devoid of all the works of reverence for God and righteousness. Again, wage a second battle [?] against your body. Bind it in confinement and fetter it with fasting. Hang it on a cross, and take its weapons away from it, namely food [?], drink, sleep [?], and rest. Afflict it with hunger, torment it with thirst, and crucify it through keeping vigil. Weary it with labors [?], and wear it down with exhaustion. Then it will be exhausted by its hunger, thirst, labor, and weariness, and it will cease its warfare against you.
